1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3.name: King's Indian Defence: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop, the move around which the whole defence is built: it pressures the centre from a distance and shelters the castled king. Black stays flexible between a classical set-up and a direct central strike, and White has to choose a set-up first.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 d5.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: with Nf3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Challenges c4 at once, before White has played Nc3. White can win space with cxd5 and then kick the recapturing knight with e4, but Black gets quick piece play against that centre; with the knight not yet on c3, this is a different game from the main Grünfeld lines.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 d6.strategy: Prepares the classical set-up: Black lets White occupy the centre with pawns and plans to undermine it later with pieces and pawn breaks. The pawn covers e5 and c5 and frees the c8 bishop, and Black keeps more options open than with a direct central strike.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 before the king's bishop is even out. White can gain space and cramp Black, which leaves an unbalanced game where Black plays against the centre from the wings, or take the pawn, which Black regains at once with piece play and a check.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and reaches the standard 3.Nc3 set-up by a different move order. White keeps every plan open, from a broad pawn centre to a fianchetto, and Black decides whether to challenge the centre at once or to build a classical structure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3.background: Viktor Korchnoi was once its most notable practitioner, and it is one of the most popular lines at grandmaster level.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3.strategy: Answers the fianchetto in kind: the bishop on g2 shelters the king and bears down on the long diagonal. Because e4 would block that bishop, White often avoids it and keeps the centre flexible, playing for a slower, patient fight instead of a big pawn centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.b4.name: King's Indian Defence: Santasiere Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.b4.strategy: An offbeat flank advance that grabs queenside space and clears b2 for the bishop. The pawn on b4 stands undefended and does nothing for the centre, so Black can complete development calmly and ask White to justify the loosening.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 O-O.strategy: Castles into the shelter of the fianchettoed bishop, so the king is safe at once. Black commits to no pawn structure yet and keeps the choice between a classical set-up and a direct strike at the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6.strategy: Prepares the classical structure, with the pawn on d6 holding the e5 square for a later central break. It usually transposes to the main line once Black castles, but it gives up the immediate central strike with the d-pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once from the wing, before castling. It is active, but d4 is defended twice and the king is still in the centre, so White can calmly continue development and Black's pawn move has no concrete follow-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 c5 5.Bg2.strategy: Ignores the challenge to d4, which is attacked once and defended twice, and completes the fianchetto. White keeps all options in the centre while Black's c-pawn has yet to find a follow-up, and the bishop will matter on the light squares and the long diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 c5 5.d5.strategy: Closes the centre instead of exchanging on c5, trading the central pawn tension for a lasting space advantage. White clamps the queenside and keeps a flexible fianchetto set-up, while the pawn on d5 becomes the target of Black's pawn breaks and the f6 knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 c5 5.dxc.strategy: Takes the pawn, but gives up the d4 pawn and with it the central grip; Black regains the c5 pawn at once with piece play and a check. Playable and harmless, yet White has only traded a centre pawn for some time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 c5 5.Bg2.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Pterodactyl Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 c5 5.Bg2.strategy: An early check that drags the queen out to pressure the queenside diagonal and the c3 square, forcing White to answer with a developing move. It gains a tempo but exposes the queen, which will have to move again, so it works only if Black gets something lasting for it.

Takes White's d-pawn at once, so White must recapture with a piece that Black's knight can then hit with tempo. Black swaps a flank pawn for a central one and gets a half-open c-file and clear targets for a sound game.

Develops with pressure on d4 and invites White to push the pawn. After d5 the knight can retreat to the edge and hit c4, the weak point of the fianchetto set-up; if White castles instead, Black keeps the choice between exchanging on d4 and holding the tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop pressures the long diagonal and shelters the future castled king. Because e4 would block it, White avoids that push and plays for a flexible, slower fight in which the bishop matters more than a pawn centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight where it watches e4 and d5 and leaves the bishop's move for later. White does not decide the pawn structure yet, so it can still choose between a slow fianchetto game and a bigger centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6 5.d5.strategy: Gains space and closes the centre at once, but commits the pawn before White's pieces are out. The pawn on d5 becomes a target for Black's pawn breaks, and the bishop on g7 gets an open diagonal towards the queenside as soon as the f6 knight moves.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6 5.Bg2.strategy: Castles into the fianchetto with the classical pawn structure in place. Black has a solid, compact set-up, and with a fianchettoed bishop on each side the fight for the centre is fought by piece pressure rather than by early pawn advances.

Develops with pressure on d4 and invites White to push d5, which drives the knight to a5 where it eyes c4, the weak point of the fianchetto set-up. Black plays against that square and the queenside, with the king's safety still to be settled.

Prepares to claim the centre with the e-pawn, which the knight supports from d7. The price is a c8 bishop shut in behind the knight; White meanwhile castles and decides whether to hold the tension in the centre or release it.

Castles and completes the set-up in which both kings sit behind fianchettoed bishops. White's kingside is more solid than in most King's Indian lines, so Black's usual attack on the king hardly works, and the fight is for the centre and c4.

Develops the queen's knight to its natural square, where it watches e4 and d5, and brings White's pieces into play before castling. White keeps the options of expanding with d5 or holding the pawn on d4, and lets Black declare its set-up first.
Supports c4 and e4 from d2, ready for a central pawn advance, but it blocks the c1 bishop and takes the knight away from the centre. Sound and flexible, though a little passive.

Pressures d4 and prepares to challenge the centre, and the knight can later head for the edge to bear down on c4, the weak point of the fianchetto set-up. Black trades a little comfort for lasting queenside pressure; White must keep c4 covered.

Supports the e5 advance with a piece and leaves the c-pawn and the c8-bishop untouched. Black aims to claim the centre with ...e5, the plan of the classical King's Indian, and White has to decide how to meet it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6 5.Bg2.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Yugoslav System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6 5.Bg2.strategy: Hits d4 with the c-pawn instead of the e-pawn, trading a wing pawn for a central one and moving Black's counterplay to the queenside. White decides whether to release the tension or to gain space; if the centre opens, the g7 bishop gains scope.
A restrained pawn move that supports a later ...d5 and gives the queen the b6 and a5 squares. Black claims no space yet, so White can take time to build a position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 O-O 5.Bg.strategy: Completes the fianchetto while Black has shown only the safe king. White keeps the pawn centre flexible and lets Black choose between a classical structure and a Grünfeld-style strike at the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 O-O 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the queen's knight where it watches d5 and e4, and keeps the bishop's move for later. White stays flexible between the slow fianchetto set-up and a sharper fight if Black strikes in the centre at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 O-O 5.d5.strategy: Gains space and closes the centre at once, but commits the pawn before White's pieces are out. The pawn on d5 becomes a target for Black's pawn breaks, and the g7 bishop has an open diagonal towards the queenside once the f6 knight moves.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 O-O 5.Bg.strategy: Commits to the classical King's Indian pawn structure, which holds e5 and keeps the g7 bishop behind a solid base. The game transposes to the main fianchetto line, a patient manoeuvring game.

Strikes at c4 and the centre at once, the Grünfeld idea meeting a fianchetto. With no knight on c3, White cannot easily build a big pawn centre, so the game is more balanced and manoeuvring, and Black fights for the centre with piece pressure.

Keeps both a quiet and a Grünfeld-style structure available and supports a later pawn on d5, so a capture there can be answered by the c-pawn. It commits to a solid, flexible set-up and waits to see where White puts the pieces.
Brings the king to safety before the centre is decided. White stays flexible, free to keep the tension on c4 and d4 or to exchange, and Black must now show what the c6 pawn is for.

Develops the queen's knight before castling and adds control of d5, the square the c6 pawn is aiming at. White stays flexible: it can keep the tension in the centre or exchange on d5 whenever that suits it.

Plans the second fianchetto, so that both bishops face the centre along the long diagonals and the d4 pawn is well covered. Sound but slow: it does nothing against Black's plan of striking in the centre at once.

Strikes at the centre, now backed by the c6 pawn, so a capture on d5 can be answered by recapturing with the pawn and keeping a solid pawn there. Black gets a sound structure and a long-diagonal bishop, and the game turns on pressure against c4 and d5.

Switches to a solid pawn chain, freeing the c8 bishop and covering e5, and gives up the immediate strike with the d-pawn. Black's game rests on a compact set-up and later pawn breaks, with the c6 pawn useful for queenside space.

Spends a second move on the c-pawn: it went to c6 to support ...d5, and now it challenges d4 instead. White takes on c5 and gets the better game, a pawn up for now, so the plan of the previous move is wasted.
